issues.legal_issue: A tenant continuing under a tenancy created by the original landlord cannot deny that landlord’s title at the commencement of the tenancy merely because the eviction claim is brought by a transferee, but may challenge a defect in the transferee’s title or a later loss of the original landlord’s title.
material_facts: The tenant’s father was originally in possession as a tenant of the owner.
During an earlier eviction dispute, the father entered into a fresh lease with the owner’s successor, accepted that successor as lessor, and the compromise was recorded in the proceedings.
The tenant inherited his father’s position under the tenancy.
The successor later transferred the property to the plaintiffs, and the tenant did not allege that this transfer was ineffective or that the successor later lost title.
The tenant’s defence was that the successor had never acquired title from the original owner because the property had previously been transferred to a trust.
issues.conclusion: The tenant was estopped from denying the successor’s title at the commencement of the fresh tenancy. Since the tenant challenged only that title, and not the plaintiffs’ transfer from the successor or a later loss of title, the defence was unavailable and the eviction decree stood.
issues.legal_principle: Section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 prevents a tenant, during the tenancy, from denying that the landlord under whom the tenancy began had title at that time. The rule also benefits a transferee from that landlord, although it does not bar a tenant from challenging the transferee’s derivative title, such as by showing that no effective transfer occurred, or from showing that the original landlord’s title later ended. The tenancy does not begin afresh whenever the landlord’s or tenant’s interest passes by assignment or succession. The Court relied on Kumar Krishna Prasad Lal Singha Deo v. Baraboni Coal Concern Ltd. and Tej Bhan Madan v. 11th Additional District Judge, and distinguished Mangat Ram v. Sardar Meharban Singh and D. Satyanarayana v. P. Jagdish, which concern the rule’s limits and exceptions.

rule.if: eviction_proceeding and tenancy_began_under_original_landlord and tenant_claims_through_original_tenant and plaintiff_claims_through_original_landlord and tenant_denies_original_landlord_title_at_tenancy_start and not tenant_challenges_transfer_to_plaintiff and not tenant_claims_later_loss_of_title

predicates.eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks to evict a person occupying property as a tenant.
predicates.tenancy_began_under_original_landlord: The tenant’s tenancy began under the landlord whose title is being denied.
predicates.tenant_claims_through_original_tenant: The person resisting eviction occupies through, or succeeds to the position of, the tenant who began the tenancy.
predicates.plaintiff_claims_through_original_landlo: The person seeking eviction claims the property through a transfer or succession from the landlord under whom the tenancy began.
predicates.tenant_denies_original_landlord_title_at: The tenant’s defence denies that the original landlord had title when the tenancy began.
predicates.tenant_challenges_transfer_to_plaintiff: The tenant alleges that the plaintiff did not obtain an effective transfer of title from the original landlord or that the transfer is otherwise legally ineffective.
predicates.tenant_claims_later_loss_of_title: The tenant alleges that the original landlord’s title ended after the tenancy began.
predicates.tenant_is_barred_from_denial: The tenant cannot deny the original landlord’s title at the commencement of the tenancy.

issues.definition: When an eviction proceeding is brought by a successor to the landlord under whom the tenancy began, a tenant who denies that landlord’s title at the outset, without challenging the transfer to the plaintiff or alleging a later loss of title, cannot rely on that denial.

issues.legal_issue: A court hearing a second appeal exceeds the limited scope of that appeal by redeciding a factual title dispute after sufficient independent grounds have already resolved the case, but that error does not require reversal when it cannot affect the outcome.
material_facts: The first appellate court had made a finding on whether the property had previously been transferred to a trust.
The High Court, in second appeal, considered the evidence and reversed that factual finding.
The High Court had already identified the fresh lease, the compromise petition, and the compromise decree as independent grounds supporting the plaintiffs’ case.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should not have reconsidered the title dispute on the evidence after reaching a conclusion on the independent documentary grounds. That error did not assist the appellant because the independent grounds remained sufficient to dispose of the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure limits the scope of a second appeal. The Court held that, once the independent documentary grounds were sufficient to resolve the case, the High Court should not have proceeded to decide the factual title dispute on the evidence. The judgment cites no earlier case for this procedural holding.

predicates.second_appeal: The challenged decision was made in a second appeal.
predicates.independent_grounds_sufficed: The case was already resolvable on grounds independent of the disputed factual issue.
predicates.high_court_redecided_factual_issue_on_ev: The High Court reconsidered a factual issue on the evidence after the independent grounds were sufficient to resolve the case.
predicates.procedural_error_does_not_require_revers: The error in exceeding the proper scope of the second appeal does not require reversal when it cannot affect the result.

issues.definition: In a second appeal, redeciding an evidentiary factual issue after independent grounds suffice is an error, but the error does not require reversal if those grounds still determine the outcome.
